children: Sovereign Metals (ASX:SVM; AIM:SVML; OTCQX:SVMLF) has appointed former Base Resources managing director Tim Carstens as executive chair to advance financing and development of its Kasiya rutile-graphite project in Malawi, which requires $727mn in initial investment before production can begin.

The appointment, effective November 19, follows completion of Kasiya’s definitive feasibility study (DFS) in April, although the company has yet to secure full project financing or announce a final investment decision, according to a November 16 regulatory announcement.

Carstens has more than 25 years of resources industry experience, including leading Base Resources from its establishment in 2008 until its acquisition by Energy Fuels (NYSE American:UUUU; TSX:EFR) in October 2024.

During his tenure, Base Resources financed, built and operated the Kwale mineral sands mine, Kenya’s first large-scale commercial mine, and advanced the Toliara mineral sands and rare earths project in Madagascar.
Sovereign’s managing director and chief executive, Frank Eagar, said the appointment would strengthen the company’s ability to secure financing and advance Kasiya towards construction.
“Tim’s appointment represents an inflexion point for Sovereign as we transition Kasiya from feasibility studies towards project construction and production,” Eagar said.

Kasiya, in central Malawi, contains one of the world’s largest known natural rutile deposits, alongside substantial graphite resources and potential heavy rare earth mineralisation. Rio Tinto is a strategic investor in Sovereign and provided technical input to the DFS.

The project’s April 2026 feasibility study estimates initial development expenditure of $727mn, followed by about $512mn for a second-phase expansion, bringing total development capital requirements to approximately $1.24bn.
The DFS envisages initial processing capacity of 12mn tonnes of ore annually, doubling to 24mn tonnes after expansion.
At steady-state production, Kasiya is expected to produce approximately 222,000 tonnes of natural rutile and 275,000 tonnes of graphite annually over an initial 25-year mine life.
The study estimates a pre-tax net present value of $2.2bn and annual earnings before interest, tax, depreciation and amortisation of $476mn at steady state.
These figures remain projections dependent on financing, construction, commodity prices and commercial development.
A separate scoping study released on September 9 examined potential heavy rare earth recovery, which was not included in the original rutile-graphite DFS.
Carstens said priorities would include securing permits, project financing and commercial arrangements, alongside assembling the team required to develop Kasiya.

Sovereign is pursuing discussions with development finance institutions, US government agencies and prospective customers, although binding financing and offtake commitments covering the project’s requirements have not been announced. Sovereign held AUD29.3mn in cash at the end of September and has said it is targeting a funding solution within six to nine months.

Under the board changes, outgoing chair Ben Stoikovich will step down on November 19 to concentrate on his role as chief executive of GreenX Metals (ASX:GRX; LSE:GRX), while remaining a consultant to Sovereign.
Founding director Mark Pearce is also retiring following the company’s November 18 annual general meeting.

Carstens will receive annual remuneration of AUD300,000 (about $202,000), alongside proposed performance-linked incentives comprising 2mn rights tied to financing and construction milestones and 3mn options exercisable at AUD0.60 each until November 16, 2031.
Sovereign has not confirmed a construction commencement date, with Kasiya’s development dependent on outstanding approvals, commercial agreements and financing.

title: Australian critical minerals developer Sovereign Metals appoints new chairman for its mine in Malawi
